```json
{"ranking": ["R1", "Rf", "M8"], "fault": "Input resistor R1 is about 21x too small (37.9 kOhm; about 815 kOhm expected). This makes Rf/R1 = 0.028, so the gain is -0.027 instead of about -0.0013. The fault could equally be Rf about 21x too large (about 50 Ohm expected)."}
```

- **Gain ratio:** The gain is set almost entirely by Rf/R1, since the op-amp's open-loop gain is high and its operating point is fine. 1059.2 / 37903 = 0.0279, which matches the simulated -0.0266. The target is about -0.0013, so the ratio is off by about 21x. No transistor fault could cause an error that large; the transistor sensitivities are below 1%.
- **Why R1 over Rf:** The resistor values alone can't tell which one was corrupted. The bandwidth, power and offset readings don't separate them either, because the feedback factor stays close to 1 in both cases. I ranked R1 first because a ~1 kOhm feedback resistor with a large input resistor is a plausible design for a small gain. Rf is a close second.
- **M5 in triode:** This is a side effect of the input common-mode level (0.9 V − 0.676 V ≈ 0.22 V at the tail node). It is not the injected fault, and it doesn't cause the gain failure.
